content: Cannabis sativa is a plant that has been utilized by humans for various purposes throughout history. It is valued for its fibrous material, known as hemp, its psychoactive and physiological effects, and the nutritional content of its oil-rich seeds. Different parts of the plant serve distinct purposes, and specific varieties are cultivated and harvested in unique ways depending on their intended use. Taxonomy and Varieties of Cannabis sativa Cannabis sativa subsp. sativa var. sativa The correct scientific name for this variety is Cannabis sativa L. subsp. sativa var. sativa. This group includes hemp landraces and cultivars that are primarily grown for fiber or seed production. Fiber-producing strains are typically tall and unbranched, while seed-producing strains are often shorter and may be either branched or unbranched. Some strains are monoecious, meaning they possess both male and female reproductive structures. Certified industrial hemp strains are characterized by a high cannabidiol (CBD) to tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) ratio, approximately 20:1, making them unsuitable for drug use. Cannabis sativa subsp. sativa var. spontanea The correct scientific name for this variety is Cannabis sativa L. subsp. sativa var. spontanea (Vavilov) Small & Cronq. It is synonymous with Cannabis ruderalis Janisch. This taxon includes wild or feral Cannabis plants that have lost many of their selectively bred traits and have adapted to their local environments. These plants are typically short, branchless, and flower early. They contain low levels of cannabinoids and have a low THC-to-CBD ratio, rendering them unsuitable for drug production. However, ruderalis strains are sometimes crossbred with indica drug strains to produce high-THC plants with the hardiness and reduced height of ruderalis. The term ruderal originated in the former Soviet Union to describe hemp populations that escaped cultivation and adapted to their surroundings. These plants are widespread in central and eastern Europe, including Lithuania, Belarus, Latvia, and Estonia, as well as in regions of North America, particularly the Midwest. Despite government eradication efforts, feral Cannabis plants, often referred to as ditch weed, remain abundant. Some botanists have proposed recognizing this taxon as a distinct species, Cannabis ruderalis. Cannabis sativa subsp. indica var. indica The correct scientific name for this variety is Cannabis sativa L. subsp. indica (Lam.) Small & Cronq var. indica (Lam.) Wehmer, synonymous with Cannabis indica Lam.. This taxon includes two types of Cannabis cultivated for drug production, commonly referred to as sativa and indica by Cannabis enthusiasts. Narrow-leafed sativa strains are native to the Indian subcontinent and are also cultivated in Africa, South and Central America, the Caribbean, and other marijuana-producing regions. These strains are typically tall, loosely branched, and late-maturing. Commercial growers often prefer indica/sativa hybrids due to their higher yields and shorter growth cycles. Wide-leafed indica strains are traditionally grown in northwest India, Afghanistan, and Pakistan for hashish production and may have originated in the Hindu Kush or Tian Shan mountain ranges. These plants are short, conical, densely branched, and have wide leaflets. They tend to produce a lower THC-to-CBD ratio compared to narrow-leafed strains. Commercially available varieties are often bred to produce high THC levels and low CBD levels. Anecdotal reports suggest that sativa strains produce a cerebral, clear-headed high, while indica strains induce a sedative, body-focused effect, often associated with drowsiness, reduced motor coordination, and increased appetite. However, no definitive chemical or pharmacological basis for these differences has been established. Some researchers have proposed recognizing this taxon as a distinct species, Cannabis indica. Recent genetic, morphological, and chemotaxonomic analyses have assigned narrow-leaflet and wide-leaflet drug biotypes, as well as southern and eastern Asian hemp landraces, to Cannabis indica. Cannabis sativa subsp. indica var. kafiristanica The correct scientific name for this variety is Cannabis sativa L. subsp. indica (Lam.) Small & Cronq var. kafiristanica (Vavilov) Small & Cronq, synonymous with Cannabis indica Lam. var. kafiristanica Vavilov. This taxon includes wild or feral plants primarily found in the Indian subcontinent and other regions where Cannabis is cultivated for drug use and has escaped cultivation. These plants may exhibit low, moderate, or high THC levels relative to CBD. They are also known to contain relatively high levels of Δ9-tetrahydrocannabidivarin (THCV) and/or cannabidivarin (CBDV). Compared to var. spontanea, these plants are often taller, more branched, and produce smaller achenes (fruits). The inflorescences of female plants are typically elongated, and the fruits detach from the plant as they mature. Common Uses of Cannabis The tough fibers of Cannabis, cultivated as hemp, are widely used in textiles. Its seeds, often used as bird feed, are a valuable source of protein. The flowers, and to a lesser extent the leaves, stems, and seeds, contain psychoactive and physiologically active compounds called cannabinoids. These compounds are consumed for recreational, medicinal, and spiritual purposes. Cannabis preparations, such as marijuana (flowers and leaves) and hashish (resinous extracts), are commonly smoked, vaporized, or ingested orally. Historically, Cannabis has also been prepared as tinctures, teas, and ointments. Plant Physiology Cannabis is a sexually reproducing plant. Female flowers are arranged in racemes and can produce hundreds of seeds. Male plants shed pollen and die weeks before the seeds on female plants ripen. While genetic factors determine a plant's sex, environmental factors, such as light cycles, can influence sexual expression. Naturally occurring monoecious plants, which have both male and female reproductive structures, may be sterile or fertile. Artificially induced hermaphrodites can have fully functional reproductive organs. Feminized seeds, sold by commercial suppliers, are derived from artificially hermaphroditic females that lack the male gene or are treated with hormones or silver thiosulfate. During the vegetative growth phase, Cannabis requires 18 hours of light and 6 hours of darkness. Flowering occurs when darkness exceeds 12 hours per day, and water is reduced. The flowering cycle lasts 4 to 6 weeks, depending on the strain and environmental conditions. The optimal soil pH for Cannabis is 6.5 to 7.2, while in hydroponic systems, the nutrient solution should have a pH of 5.2 to 5.8. This pH range is hostile to most bacteria and fungi, making Cannabis well-suited for hydroponic cultivation. Pharmacology The primary psychoactive compound in Cannabis is Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). The plant contains approximately 60 cannabinoids, most of which are present in trace amounts. Cannabidiol (CBD), a non-psychoactive cannabinoid, can block the effects of THC in the nervous system. Differences in the chemical composition of Cannabis varieties may result in varying effects on humans. Synthetic THC, such as dronabinol, lacks CBD, cannabinol (CBN), and other cannabinoids, which may explain its differing pharmacological effects compared to natural Cannabis. Most commercially available Cannabis contains less than 8% THC, but selective breeding and modern cultivation techniques, such as hydroponics, have produced varieties with THC levels exceeding 15%. Varieties with less than 1% THC, typically cultivated for hemp, may cause mild lightheadedness or headaches but do not produce intoxication. Female plants produce significantly more resin than male plants, and unpollinated female flowers (sinsemilla) have higher THC content than seeded flowers.
